description: We are a family team of Space enthusiasts.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is an old-style wooden jukebox that runs in your web browser. Press a big red button to pick a record, and it plays a NASA picture of Earth's ocean or atmosphere as live music while the picture stays on screen. We read the colours in NASA images as data (sea temperature, salinity, density, ocean currents, aerosols, lightning and the 2025/2026 El Niño) and turn them into sound. A beam sweeps left to right, height on the map is pitch, and every kind of data has its own instrument. Drums change with the region under the beam and speed up where the data is stronger, and the music slides from hopeful to sad to urgent as the data gets more extreme.

The El Niño page switches between a week in 2025 and the same week in 2026, so you can hear the tropical Pacific warm. Our decode of NASA's pictures follows NOAA's weekly Niño 3.4 index (correlation 0.994).

Most Earth data only comes as pictures, which shuts out blind and low-vision people. So there is a spoken guide, a "Hear Me" mode that reads each screen aloud, text descriptions of every picture, full keyboard control, and "Hear voices", which plays each instrument alone with its label. Scrolling sheet music, a "Data and limits" panel for every record and an exportable note trace show how each sound was made. Nothing to install.
details:
Project link: https://astropi-9.github.io/space-apps-challenge-earth-jukebox/ (best on computer)

What it does Earth Jukebox is a jukebox with six records. Each one takes a NASA visualisation, reads its colours as numbers, and plays those numbers as music while you watch the picture.

  • Sea temperature, salinity and density (NASA SVS 3652): a still map with a beam that sweeps west to east, or a movie of the Earth turning.
  • Ocean currents and Year of the ocean (NASA SVS 3912): a whole year of sea surface temperature and currents. "Follow a current" lets you pick a current, such as the Gulf Stream or the Kuroshio, and hear it traced along the picture's own flow lines.
  • Aerosols (NASA SVS 5669): smoke, dust, sea salt and sulphate.
  • Lightning (NASA SVS 5011): every flash seen from the International Space Station becomes a drum hit.
  • El Niño, a third version of Sea temperature (NASA SVS 5683, "Signs of El Nino in 2026"): how much warmer or cooler than normal the tropical Pacific is (the colour bar runs from minus 4 °C, blue, through pale cream, normal, to plus 4 °C, dark red). One page with a 10 Oct 2025 / 10 Oct 2026 switch lets you hear a beam sweep from Indonesia to South America on either date. In 2026 a broad band of water more than 3 °C above normal runs along the equator; in 2025 the equator was slightly cooler than normal. The mood of the music is ranked against both years together, so 2026 sounds more urgent and 2025 calmer. The El Niño pages have their own sound: a cello leads the strong anomalies over brass chords and timpani rolls, and the two deepest reds get a low double bass chord (medium-dark red, 2.5 to 3.5 °C above normal) and a low timpani rumble (almost black-red, 3.5 °C and above), both getting louder with more deep red and fading at the South American coast.

How it works Left to right is time. Top to bottom is latitude, and latitude is pitch, so north sounds high. Each kind of data has its own voice: a drone, chords, a high voice, a lead melody with Carnatic-style ornaments (gamakas), and drums. The drums are regional (tabla, djembe, taiko, darbuka and others) and play faster where the data is stronger. The scale changes with the region under the beam, and the mood moves from hopeful to sad to urgent as the data gets stronger. We read values off NASA's own colour bars and sum them onto a grid of 160 columns by 18 latitude bands. The sound is made live in your browser with the Web Audio API. Some instrument sounds were rendered with MuseScore 4.

Built like a real jukebox We designed it to look and feel like a classic jukebox, on purpose. There's a wooden cabinet, big red buttons for each record, a second page where you choose a version, and double doors that swing open on the record you pick and close again when the song ends. Old jukeboxes are covered in buttons, so the switches around the map are chunky, labelled and clearly ON or OFF, like the controls on the real thing. The two that matter most, "Narration" and "Hear voices", have a gold rim so a first-time visitor knows where to start.

Making it understandable and accessible

  • "Hear voices" plays each voice on its own, with a label, so you can learn what each one means.
  • Scrolling sheet music shows every note as it plays.
  • Each record has a "Data and limits" panel that says where the data came from, how we decoded it, and what not to conclude from it.
  • You can export a note trace (CSV or JSON) that links each note to the column, month or path step that produced it, with a SHA-256 fingerprint of each source file.
  • There's a spoken guided tour, a "Hear Me" mode that reads each screen aloud, text descriptions of every picture, full keyboard control, and a mute for each voice.

What we hope it achieves We want people, especially blind and low-vision people, to be able to hear Earth's ocean and atmosphere, and we want patterns like the seasons, El Niño and storm regions to be easier to notice and to teach, without any special software.

How we checked it We checked that our decoding behaves like the real thing. Turning a colour back into a temperature and comparing it with NASA's colour bar is accurate to about 0.05 °C. The decoded ocean comes out at about 29 °C at the equator and about 1 °C near the poles. In the year-long ocean record, the northern and southern mid-latitudes warm and cool in opposite seasons (correlation -0.95): the north peaks in late August and early September and the south in late February and early March, with swings of about 4.5 to 4.8 °C at mid-latitudes and under 1 °C in the tropics. For El Niño, the Niño 3.4 region decoded from NASA's pictures follows NOAA's weekly Niño 3.4 index with a correlation of 0.994 from 29 January to 10 October 2026 and 0.83 over the same dates in 2025 (the decode runs about 0.4 °C warm in 2026). On 10 October 2026 it decodes to +3.35 °C against NOAA's +3.2 °C. We also ran the sound code over every column of every record without errors, and measured the mix so every record sits within about 2 dB of the others in loudness.

Limits, honestly The values are decoded from rendered pictures. The values come from NASA's own colour bars, but how they become sound is an artistic interpretation: we map the colour and position of each part of the picture to pitch, instruments and rhythm by our own choices. We balanced the mix by measuring it. Tested in Chromium-based browsers and Safari; Firefox is untested.

Tools HTML, JavaScript, the Web Audio API and Canvas; PowerShell and Python (numpy, scipy, Pillow, ffmpeg) for the decoding and checking scripts; MuseScore 4 for instrument sounds and loops; Claude Code for development (see the next section).
